summary: Fictional 1,208-participant randomized clinical trial (TEXT-BP) of automated tailored text messaging vs attention control on 12-month systolic blood pressure in 12 US community health centers.

defects.find:
**Importance:** Uncontrolled hypertension is common among adults who receive care in community health centers, and poor medication adherence is a modifiable contributor. Whether low-cost automated text messaging improves blood pressure in this setting is uncertain.

**Objective:** To determine whether 12 months of automated, tailored text messages improves systolic blood pressure (SBP) compared with attention-control messages.

**Design, Setting, and Participants:** Parallel-group randomized clinical trial at 12 federally qualified community health centers in Ohio. Adults aged 18 to 80 years with office SBP of 140 mm Hg or higher taking at least 1 antihypertensive medication were enrolled from March 2022 to August 2023; final follow-up was in September 2024.

**Interventions:** Participants were randomized 1:1 to tailored text messaging (adherence reminders, education, and 2-way refill prompts; n = 604) or attention-control messages (monthly general health messages; n = 604), each added to usual care.

defects.find: Blood pressure at baseline, 6 months, and 12 months was measured by trained research assistants who were not involved in recruitment or intervention delivery and who were masked to group assignment; participants were asked not to disclose their messages.
defects.replace: Blood pressure at baseline, 6 months, and 12 months was measured by the health center nurse care coordinators, who also enrolled participants and responded to flagged text-message replies and were therefore aware of group assignment.
defects.description: The primary outcome (office SBP) is measured by unmasked staff who deliver part of the intervention, creating detection/observer bias in an open-label trial.

defects.find: The primary analysis followed the intention-to-treat principle and included all 1,208 randomized participants in the group to which they were assigned, regardless of the number of messages received or opt-out. The 12-month change in SBP was compared between groups with linear regression adjusted for the stratification factors (health center and baseline SBP stratum) and baseline SBP, with heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors. Missing 12-month values were handled with multiple imputation by chained equations under a missing-at-random assumption, using 20 imputed data sets that included baseline characteristics, 6-month blood pressure, and adherence, with estimates combined by Rubin's rules (Rubin, 1987; White et al., 2011).
defects.replace: The primary analysis was restricted to the per-protocol population: participants who did not opt out of messaging and who attended the 12-month visit. Participants without a 12-month measurement were excluded; an intention-to-treat analysis with multiple imputation (Rubin, 1987; White et al., 2011) was not performed because the per-protocol population best reflects the effect among engaged users. The 12-month change in SBP was compared between groups with linear regression adjusted for the stratification factors (health center and baseline SBP stratum) and baseline SBP, with heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors.
defects.description: The primary analysis is per-protocol/complete-case only with no intention-to-treat analysis or principled handling of the 9% missing outcomes, so randomization is broken and the effect may be biased.

defects.find: The prespecified primary outcome, unchanged from the registered protocol, was the change in office SBP from baseline to 12 months. Prespecified secondary outcomes were change in office DBP at 12 months; change in SBP at 6 months; BP control, defined as office blood pressure below 140/90 mm Hg at 12 months;
defects.replace: The primary outcome was BP control, defined as office blood pressure below 140/90 mm Hg at 12 months; this outcome replaced change in office SBP, the primary outcome in the trial registration, after review of the 6-month data. Secondary outcomes were change in office SBP and DBP at 12 months; change in SBP at 6 months;
defects.description: The primary outcome was switched from the registered SBP change to BP control after an unblinded look at interim data, a post hoc outcome switch that invalidates the confirmatory claim.

defects.find: In this randomized clinical trial among adults with uncontrolled hypertension receiving care in community health centers, automated tailored text messaging added to usual care modestly reduced SBP at 12 months compared with attention-control messages. Longer follow-up is needed to determine whether the effect is sustained and whether it reduces cardiovascular events.
defects.replace: In this randomized clinical trial, automated tailored text messaging lowered blood pressure enough to prevent strokes and myocardial infarctions, and it should be adopted as standard care for all adults with hypertension in all practice settings, where it can replace pharmacist- and nurse-led adherence programs.
defects.description: The Conclusions claim prevention of cardiovascular events (never measured; 12-month surrogate outcome only) and universal generalizability from 1 Ohio safety-net network, overstating the evidence.
